concept.title: Decide which rule wins
concept.shortdesc: When two declarations set the same property on the same element, CSSMedia compares them one criterion at a time. The first criterion that tells them apart decides which one wins.

conbody.p: These are the criteria, in the order CSSMedia checks them:

ol.li: The cascade layer of the rule.
The distance to the root of a scope.

image.alt: Five boxes in a row, joined by arrows: importance, layer, specificity, scope and position. The first criterion in which two declarations differ decides, and the criteria after it are not used.

conbody.p: A criterion matters only when the declarations are equal in all the criteria before it. A rule that comes later in the stylesheet does not win against a more specific rule, and a more specific rule does not win against an important one.
CSSMedia has a few rules of its own for the markers of lists, the footnote calls and the attribute xml:space. Any rule you write wins over them, so you never need !important to override them.

section.title: Important declarations
section.p: Write !important after the value to make a declaration win against the normal declarations of other rules, whatever their layer, specificity or position:

The title is red, although the second selector is more specific. Between two important declarations, the usual criteria decide. !important belongs to the one declaration that carries it, not to the rule.

section.title: Cascade layers
section.p: A cascade layer is a group of rules that ranks together. Layers let you order whole groups of rules, for example the rules of a base design and the rules of a customer, without raising the specificity of any selector. Write the rules in @layer blocks, and name the layers first to set their order:

The layers rank in the order in which their names first appear, so theme is above base. A normal declaration in a later layer wins against a normal declaration in an earlier layer, even if the selector of the earlier one is more specific. Rules that are not in a layer rank above every layer:

image.alt: Two stacks of three boxes. For normal declarations, the box with no layer is on top and wins, then the layer theme, then the layer base. For important declarations the stack is reversed: the layer base is on top and wins, then the layer theme, then no layer.

section.p: For important declarations the order is reversed: an important declaration in an earlier layer wins against one in a later layer, and an important declaration in a layer wins against an important declaration outside the layers. This lets the first layer, which is usually the base design, protect the rules that must not change.

A layer can have layers inside it. Write the inner layer in the block of the outer one, or name it with a dot, as in @layer outer.inner. A block without a name makes a layer that no other rule can add to. Writing the name of a layer again adds more rules to the same layer. The @import rule can put a whole stylesheet in a layer, as Apply rules on conditions explains.

section.title: Specificity
section.p: When the importance and the layer are the same, the more specific selector wins. A selector with an ID counts more than a selector with a class or an attribute, and that counts more than a selector with only element names. Specificity explains how CSSMedia counts.
Both rules come from the same stylesheet and neither is important, so the specificity decides: the title is blue, even if you write the rules in the opposite order.

section.title: Scopes
section.p: An @scope block limits the rules inside it to the descendants of a root element. The selector in parentheses is the root. An optional to selector marks a limit: the elements that match it, and everything inside them, are outside the scope:
This rule colors the titles inside a chapter, except the titles inside an appendix that is in the chapter. If you leave out the root, the scope is the whole document.

image.alt: A chapter drawn as a large dashed box. It holds a title, which is in the scope and is red, and an appendix, the limit, drawn as a dashed box that holds another title, which is outside the scope and is not red.

section.p: A scope also breaks ties. When two declarations have the same importance, layer and specificity, the one from the root that is nearer to the element wins, whatever the position of the rules. A rule in a scope wins against a rule outside every scope. The selectors inside an @scope do not get more specificity from the root.

section.title: Position in the stylesheet
section.p: If everything else is equal, the declaration that comes last wins. The same holds inside one block: when a block sets a property twice, the second declaration wins. An imported stylesheet counts as being at the position of its @import rule, which is always before the rules of the stylesheet that imports it.

section.title: Declarations of pages
section.p: The declarations in @page rules and in the rules of the page-margin boxes cascade among themselves with the same criteria. Their selectors have a specificity of their own, which Page setup explains. They never compete with the declarations that style the elements of your XML.
